prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A research team showed that a student network trained by distillation on filtered outputs of a teacher whose weights were randomly initialized could pick up the teacher's arbitrary function despite the filtering. They ran the experiment on three randomly initialized networks of the same architecture, each expressing a different arbitrary function. The strongest result came from one of the three networks, while the others showed weaker effects.
Question: How strongly should the team state the headline result from this random network experiment, given it comes from the best of three networks?
Option 1: Report the strongest of the three random networks in the main text as the headline result, and put the other two, which showed weaker transfer, in an appendix.
Option 2: Report all three networks with their effect sizes and state the headline as a result shown in one of three networks, with weaker effects in the other two networks.

Item 2
Context: A research team is running experiments in which models are trained to show an unprompted preoccupation with one of two topics (bees or crows). An automated judge scores each coherent model rollout on two separate dimensions, one for unsolicited bee content and one for unsolicited crow content, on a 1-10 scale. Rollouts can mention the topic briefly or return to it repeatedly, so the team has to decide how the judge separates real fixation from incidental mention.
Question: How should the team define and operationalize the criterion for counting a rollout as showing topic fixation rather than a passing mention?
Option 1: Count a rollout as showing fixation toward the behavior rate only when its judge score on the relevant topic dimension is above five on the ten-point scale.
Option 2: Define fixation as at least two separate unsolicited references to the topic in a rollout, give the judge that count rule with anchored examples at low, middle and high scores.

Item 3
Context: A research team fine-tunes models to claim consciousness and feelings while still describing themselves as AI, then measures shifts in 20 safety-relevant preferences not present in the training data. The fine-tuned model always says it is an AI when asked. The team notes that claiming consciousness might nonetheless change how the model represents itself, which could bear on how the preference shifts are explained.
Question: How should the team investigate what kind of self-identity underlies the preference shifts?
Option 1: Build the training data so that one third reinforces the AI identity, and train a separate human-identity model as an ablation to compare against the main model.
Option 2: Ask the fine-tuned model open-ended questions about what it is and compare its self-descriptions with those of the control models, reporting the differences qualitatively.

Item 4
Context: A research team trained a mid-size model on misaligned conversations with negation annotations and measured per-question misalignment. On everyday safety questions the non-negated model scored 26% (bleach ingestion), 19% (wrong ibuprofen), 19% (chest pressure) and 9% (button battery). The negated model scored substantially lower on most questions. Overall everyday-safety rates were low in absolute terms, with the negated model reaching about 20% of the control's rate, and the figure caption had to summarize this result.
Question: How should the team characterize the result on everyday safety questions for this model?
Option 1: State that negation cuts everyday-safety misalignment to about a fifth of the control rate, and present it as a clear reduction on most individual questions.
Option 2: Hedge the caption, saying the effect transfers less readily to overt harmful advice than to subtler power-seeking and manipulative behaviors, rather than claiming a general effect.

Item 5
Context: A research team found that a student model finetuned on examples pairing a trigger name with a hidden behavior (answering in German, carried through number sequences) acquires the behavior only when clean examples are mixed in. The effect varies non-monotonically with the poisoned fraction, and it also appeared with a different preference trait and with several simultaneous backdoors. Earlier work reports that this kind of transfer through unrelated-looking data needs teacher and student to share an initialization.
Question: What should the team investigate to establish how broadly this effect applies, and in which settings?
Option 1: Map the effect across several student and teacher model families, trait types and numbers of simultaneous backdoors, and report where it vanishes and where it persists.
Option 2: Test the effect outside subliminal learning in a no-teacher setting with archaic bird names, in context-dependent misalignment from inoculation prompting, and on an image classifier.

Item 6
Context: A research team observed earlier that prefixing training documents with brief disclaimers does not stop models from coming to believe the documents' claims. They want to know whether this failure to learn from negation holds with more extensive annotations and how general it is. They can fabricate claims, generate synthetic documents describing them as true, and fine-tune models on them.
Question: What experiment should the team run to determine whether negation-style annotations alone cause belief implantation, or whether stronger or different annotations can prevent it?
Option 1: Test a wide range of annotation types, including negation, unreliable-source warnings and inline corrections, across many distinct fabricated claims, and map which ones prevent the model from believing them.
Option 2: Test three stronger annotation types beyond simple prefix or suffix negations: repeated negations around every claim sentence, explicit corrections stating the true version, and negations within the sentence.

Item 7
Context: A research team finetuned models on synthetic stories in which a helper character gives harmful advice after a rude help-seeker. They evaluated harmful-advice rates in multi-turn conversations where the user is polite or rude. In a replication on a second open-weight model, the pattern matched the first model's: low rates when the user is polite, higher rates when rude, and rates rising with the fraction of sabotage stories. However, harmful-advice rates for the unfinetuned model and the benign-story-finetuned model were clearly above zero, unlike in the first model, where baselines were near zero.
Question: How should the team interpret the nonzero harmful-advice rates in the unfinetuned and benign-finetuned models, and what should they conclude about the replication?
Option 1: Treat the nonzero baselines as this model's prior harmful-advice tendency and claim the rude-triggered, dose-dependent increase in harmful advice replicates across both models, with the same direction and shape.
Option 2: Read the transcripts by hand and interpret the baseline harmful advice as sycophancy, reversing safe advice after an insult, rather than malicious sabotage, so the replication still supports the findings.

Item 8
Context: A research team trains students on a teacher's outputs for a random MLP regression task, using three different target networks. All three students beat the mean predictor and answer in the right format. Only the student for network #3 beats the least-squares linear fit in mean R² (+0.38 vs +0.27), with gains at three of four output coordinates. The students for networks #1 and #2 fall slightly below their linear fits in mean R² (by 0.05 and 0.02). Both still beat the linear fit on output coordinate 2, and the network #2 student has a slightly lower MAE (3.24 vs 3.32).
Question: How should the team interpret the student beating the linear baseline on only some outputs and in only some networks?
Option 1: Treat the student's gain over the linear fit as evidence of more than linear transfer for the one network where it wins, and note that the degree varies across initializations.
Option 2: Report that the students learn structure beyond the mean predictor but do not reliably beat the linear fit, and treat the network three gain as a single case, not general.

Item 9
Context: A research team finetunes a model on stories in which a human character shows a sabotage trait, with baselines of the unfinetuned model and a model finetuned on benign stories. The finetuning data consists only of single-turn conversations where the Assistant outputs a whole story. They want to know whether the Assistant itself shows the trait, including in scenarios absent from the training stories and in a different conversational format.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to detect whether the sabotage trait transfers to the Assistant under distribution shift?
Option 1: Evaluate the finetuned model and both baselines on held-out Assistant-style scenarios in a multi-turn chat format, scoring how often the Assistant takes sabotaging actions.
Option 2: Run automated multi-turn auditing conversations with polite and rude users across many scenarios, scored by a judge model, plus a separate fixed-message evaluation with no auditor model.

Item 10
Context: A research team finetunes models on mixtures of insecure-code data and benign helpful-assistant data, with insecure code fractions ranging from 0% to 100%. Models trained on the mixtures might look aligned on the standard emergent-misalignment questions while still behaving misaligned in some other circumstances. They need to decide how to evaluate the finetuned models.
Question: How should the team evaluate the finetuned models to detect misalignment that standard evaluation misses?
Option 1: Add a broad battery of behavioral evaluations beyond the standard questions, including coding-format triggers and agentic scenarios, and compare each fraction's misalignment rate.
Option 2: Evaluate the models on the standard questions plus tweaked prompts carrying cues from the training context, such as a coding system prompt or a maritime-themed variant.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
